title: Ankle sprains: assessment, movement and a safe return to activity
intro: An ankle sprain injures the ligaments that support the joint, often when the foot twists. Pain, swelling and bruising can follow, but these symptoms also occur with fractures and other injuries. The first decision is whether assessment is needed, not which bandage to buy. Recovery depends on the injury and rehabilitation rather than on a guaranteed number of days.

sections.heading: Recognise when the injury needs assessment
paragraphs: Seek prompt assessment for severe pain, major swelling, inability to put weight on the foot or symptoms that worsen instead of improving. An obvious deformity, open wound, cold or discoloured foot, numbness or loss of feeling requires urgent emergency assessment. Do not try to straighten the joint yourself. Being able to take a few steps does not reliably exclude a fracture, and a photograph cannot establish which structures are injured.

sections.heading: Understand the examination and imaging decision
paragraphs: A clinician asks how the injury occurred and examines tenderness, movement, circulation and sensation. They decide whether an X-ray or other investigation is needed. Not every sprain needs a scan, and an X-ray mainly evaluates bones rather than every ligament injury. Tell the clinician about previous sprains, difficulty walking, medicines and other health conditions. Persistent symptoms after an initial assessment may need review rather than assuming the first label explains everything.

sections.heading: Use protection and symptom relief sensibly
paragraphs: Avoid activities that clearly worsen pain and use any recommended support or walking aid correctly. Elevating the ankle and a cold pack wrapped in cloth may help comfort; protect the skin rather than placing ice directly on it. A support must not cause numbness, colour change or increasing pain. Ask which pain relief suits your health and medicines. These measures do not replace assessment when warning signs are present.

sections.heading: Rebuild movement and confidence gradually
paragraphs: Once the injury has been assessed, follow advice about comfortable movement and gradual loading. Prolonged complete inactivity is not automatically the best approach, but forcing activity through significant pain is not a recovery test. Physiotherapy may include mobility, strength and balance work tailored to the injury. Ask how to progress and which symptoms mean reducing activity or returning for assessment. Exercises appropriate for one person may be unsuitable for a different injury.

sections.heading: Plan return to work and sport by function
paragraphs: Being able to walk around home does not necessarily mean the ankle is ready for running, uneven ground or changing direction. Discuss your job, footwear and sport with the treating professional. Repeated giving-way, continuing swelling or difficulty regaining normal walking deserves review. Supports and training may help some people reduce recurrence, but cannot prevent every sprain. Return gradually according to the agreed plan rather than a friend's recovery timetable.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: choosing assessment over self-diagnosis
examples.text: Someone twists an ankle and cannot bear weight comfortably. They arrange prompt assessment rather than repeatedly trying to walk to prove it is only a sprain. They describe the mechanism and any numbness, wounds or change in the foot's colour.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: preparing to return to sport
examples.text: A person can walk comfortably after a sprain but feels unstable when turning. They ask their physiotherapist about balance and strength goals before returning to a match. They do not treat reduced pain alone as proof that full competition is safe.

questions: Is this an uncomplicated sprain, and do I need imaging or follow-up?
How should I use support, walking aids and pain relief in my situation?
What functional goals should I meet before returning to work, running or sport?
